patch.value: The catalog completeness gate cannot fail in CI, and a package it should have caught has been missing since it was created

pm-web carries a test whose stated purpose is the completeness direction that the other catalog tests do not cover: every pm extension present in the fleet must appear in the catalog, so a package added to the fleet cannot be silently missing from the UI. It derives the expected set from the fleet directory rather than restating it as a second list, which is the right design and is explicitly explained in the test.

It cannot fire where it matters. The test opens with an early return when the fleet siblings are not resolvable, and in CI pm-web is checked out standalone with no sibling directories, so the derived set is empty and the assertion is skipped. The gate therefore passes vacuously on every pull request and only ever runs on a developer machine that happens to have the whole fleet cloned beside it. A gate that cannot fail in the environment that guards the merge is not a gate.

It was measured, not theorised: running the suite locally with the fleet present fails with actual ['pm-ado'] against expected [], and pm-ado has been in the fleet with a manifest.json declaring five capabilities since it was created. Every pm-web CI run over that period was green.

There is a second, independent problem in the same area. The sibling availability test decides whether a package is publishable by asking whether its package.json declares publishConfig.access. That is a convention rather than a measurement, and pm-ado already breaks it: it declares publishConfig.access public while being release-gated behind vars.PM_RELEASE_APPROVED and absent from npm, so cataloguing it by that rule would render an install button for a package npm answers 404 for — the exact outcome the assertion's own message says it exists to prevent.

pm-ado appears in the catalog with an availability that matches its real installability; the completeness assertion fails a CI run when a fleet package is absent from the catalog, demonstrated by a deliberate omission on a branch rather than argued; the availability rule is decided by something that measures whether publication can happen rather than by the presence of a package.json convention; and no gate in this area retains an early return that turns absence of input into a pass

value.author: codex
value.text:
Measured the blindness rather than reasoning about it, and it is worse than the item first recorded: two gates degrade to tautologies in a CI checkout, not one.

The completeness assertion returns early when the fleet siblings are unresolvable, which is every CI run. The membership assertion is worse in kind: EXPECTED_NAMES is defined as FLEET_EXTENSIONS when siblings resolve and catalogNames() otherwise, so in CI it compares the catalog against itself and can only ever pass. Both were green throughout the period pm-ado sat in the fleet with a manifest declaring five capabilities and no catalog entry.

The fix gives the gate an input that exists in CI. A committed snapshot at test/fleet-extensions.snapshot.json records every fleet extension with its manifest description, its package.json description, its sorted capabilities and whether it declares publishConfig; a new assertion reads it and fails when the catalog omits an entry, misdescribes one, or declares an availability the package contradicts. The snapshot is an input and never the source of truth: a companion assertion re-derives it from the live fleet wherever the siblings resolve, so a stale snapshot fails loudly instead of quietly narrowing what CI checks, and the generator refuses to write an empty snapshot because an empty one would restore exactly the vacuous pass it was written to remove.

Proved the new gate fires by deleting the pm-ado entry from the catalog and running the suite: it fails with the missing package named. A gate that cannot be shown to fail is indistinguishable from one that cannot fail.

pm-ado is now catalogued as unreleased, which required a change in pm-ado itself: it declared publishConfig.access while being release-gated and absent from npm, so cataloguing it by the existing rule would have rendered an install button for a package npm answers 404 for. That is tracked as pm-ado-tg1f and shipped separately.

The derivation module is covered at 100 percent lines, branches and functions against a synthetic tree rather than the real siblings, because every real package is well formed and reading them would only ever exercise the happy path.

value.author: codex
value.text:
Both review findings on the first round were valid, and both attacked the same weakness in the mechanism rather than a detail of it.

Greptile's point was that malformed fleet metadata was silently omitted or coerced to publishable false, and that because generation refuses only an entirely empty result while the freshness assertion repeats the same derivation, a future snapshot could omit an extension and nothing would notice. That is exactly the failure this mechanism was written to remove, reintroduced one level down: a manifest that fails to parse looks identical to a package that is not there, and two consumers of one lossy function agree on the same wrong answer. The derivation now returns what it could not read alongside what it could. Generation refuses to write when anything is unreadable, and the freshness assertion fails on the same condition, so an unparseable manifest is a defect to fix rather than a package to drop.

CodeRabbit's point was sharper and I had half-made it myself without following it through. availability was being asserted against publishConfig, which is an intent to publish, while the catalog contract defines published as npm-installable. Those are different questions, and the gap between them is precisely how this catalog came to promise an install for a package the registry answers 404 for. Aligning pm-ado's package.json fixed today's instance and left the gate unable to catch the next one.

The snapshot now records what the registry actually serves, queried at generation time. That is the right moment for the question: regenerating is a deliberate online act, while the gate that reads the snapshot must work on an offline runner. Generation refuses to write when the registry cannot be reached for any package, because falling back to publishConfig for exactly those would reinstate the proxy this field replaces, and treating unreachable as unpublished would relabel the whole fleet the moment a runner lost the network. The freshness assertion compares only the locally derivable fields, since re-deriving registry state would either need the network on every test run or report a false mismatch offline.

Measured after the change: 20 extensions, 17 served by npm, and the three that are not are the three release-gated packages pm-ado, pm-rl and pm-vcs. Coverage on the derivation module stays at 100 percent lines, branches and functions.

One process note worth keeping. The new tests passed under tsx --test and the failure only appeared in npm run coverage, because tsx does not typecheck and the build:test step does. A stale type annotation on the snapshot had survived the return-shape change. Running the fast runner alone would have shipped it.

patch.value: Committed fleet snapshot as the gate's input, with unreadable metadata reported and generation refusing to write on it, and npm publication state recorded at generation time so the offline gate asserts a fact rather than a proxy.
The gate fails in a standalone CI checkout when the catalog omits a package, misdescribes one, or declares an availability npm contradicts.

Proved to fire by deleting the pm-ado entry. 20 extensions recorded, 17 served by npm; the three that are not are the release-gated pm-ado, pm-rl and pm-vcs. Coverage holds at 100 percent on the derivation module and the gate reports 30 source files with thresholds met.

The completeness gate reads a committed snapshot so it has input in CI, the derivation reports unreadable metadata instead of skipping it, and availability is asserted against what npm actually serves rather than against publishConfig.
